TLDR: I took a little look at clinicaltrials(dot)gov to see what trials are ongoing for HCQ. Voat doesn't like me posting links. Go to the website, search for COVID as the disease and Plaquenil as the treatment to reproduce my search. I saw nothing nefarious in any of the study designs I looked at.

Lots of trials, both foreign and domestic. There are 62 trials currently recruiting or active right now including dozens in the US. I looked through a sample of the US studies available (see below) and didn't see anything nefarious as anon alleges in the 8kun post. I have run across one study that uses Vitamin C as a placebo which is definitely a bad design given that high-dose Vit C is actively being researched in sepsis and conditions of hyperactive immune response, but I saw nothing of the sort in any study currently ongoing. It's good to keep an eye on these things though. Even the "high doses" were reasonable and can be explained by pharmacokinetics of the drug or by a specific nuance of the study design that is logical.

A sample of six studies briefly evaluated below:

-Study at Intermountain Health: HCQ vs AZ for treatment - protocols are within the normal range of dosing for both drugs. Inclusion criteria select for cases severe enough to require hospital admission. Exclusion criteria are reasonable for both drugs. Appears to be a properly designed study, though I'm unsure why they're comparing vs AZ rather than placebo. They're also going open label (creates bias), likely in order to get results faster since they don't have time to manufacture a proper placebo for both drugs. AZ's antiviral activity is largely theoretical and in vitro only. It's mainly an antibiotic. Didier Raoult (the famous French study) used AZ in addition to HCQ to prevent secondary bacterial infection which is common following viral pneumonia.

-University of Chicago study: HCQ for outpatient treatment of high-risk COVID patient - this is a small study, only 20 patients, but the kicker is that they're using 1200 mg HCQ daily, 3x the routine dose. The authors do note that this is a tolerability study, which explains why they would opt for only 20 patients and for the high dose. It's a quick study to assess the extremes of safety. They're specifically recruiting high-risk patients with mild symptoms, and exclusion criteria are reasonable and prudent.

-Queen's Medical Center Honolulu study: HCQ vs standard of care in COVID patients. This is a broad study including any patient status with positive diagnosis whether treated inpatient or outpatient. Dosing is appropriate: 200 mg twice daily for 5 days, and the study appears to be properly designed to assess clinically meaningful outcomes. Didier Raoult's study looked at viral counts, not clinical outcomes (like whether a patient needed oxygen, mechanical ventilation, or expired)

-Baylor University study: HCQ for prophylaxis in healthcare workers with high risk of exposure. This one uses a prophylaxis regimen similar to malaria: loading dose + weekly dose for 7 weeks. Inclusion criteria are broad as would be expected. Exclusion criteria are reasonable.

-Hackensack Medical Center, NJ study: HCQ for prophylaxis in healthcare workers with high risk of exposure. Same regimen as the Baylor study. Exclusion criteria hit the main points, but it's clear they're not as academic as the University teaching hospitals with their study proposal. It's still a viable and meaningful design.

-Rutger's University study: HCQ + AZ vs HCQ alone for treatment. Dose here is 600 mg/day vs 400, but that's what Didier Raoult did, so it's quite reasonable to use this dose. Primary outcome is viral load, so not as helpful as clinical outcomes, but they're assessed as secondaries. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are fine.
